evidence.quote: In 2025, we wrote extensively about how datacenter capacity was the bottleneck for AI compute growth. evidence.quote: AI Debt Financing will become a multi-trillion-dollar credit market, with over $7T of debt outstanding by 2029 driven both by AI IT Capex and AI Datacenter Capex needs for Neoclouds, datacenter builders, and even hyperscalers. This will make it the second largest asset backed debt market after the US mortgage-backed financing market at just over $13T.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis forecasts more than $7 trillion of AI debt outstanding by 2029, making it the second-largest asset-backed debt market after the just-over-$13 trillion US mortgage-backed market.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: Annual AI Capex – including GPUs, networking, storage and attached CPU compute as well as for the Datacenters to house AI compute – will be well north of $2T in 2028.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis forecasts annual AI capital expenditures, including AI IT equipment and data centers, will exceed $2 trillion in calendar 2028.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: Inference providers in particular are very contracted time sensitive compared to training focused AI Labs. While AI Labs are able to commit for longer periods like 3 years and beyond, inference providers are completely unwilling to sign for longer than 1y and would rather forego access to compute than take the risk of committing for any extended period of time.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis says AI labs will commit to compute contracts of three years or longer, while inference providers will not sign for more than one year.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: At this point, we are only aware of a few Neoclouds that are still offering 1y rentals, and they are setting aggressive terms for rental – sometimes requiring prepays of up to 100% of the total contract value.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis says only a few neoclouds still offer one-year rentals, sometimes requiring customers to prepay up to 100% of the contract value.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: In 2025, we wrote extensively about how datacenter capacity was the bottleneck for AI compute growth. By early 2026, the datacenter supply situation improved considerably, but it became clear that chip production was now the limiting constraint. Now – mid-way through the year – it is clear that financing will now be one of the most significant obstacles to ramping large scale compute broadly available to everyone.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis assesses that data-center capacity was the AI-compute bottleneck in 2025, chip production became the constraint by early 2026, and financing had become a major obstacle by mid-2026.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: This is why Nvidia has stepped in and has started backstopping GPU rental offtakes themselves . In the backstop program, Nvidia provides a take-or-pay commitment to Neoclouds – a minimum revenue guarantee on the underlying GPU capacity. In exchange for this backstop, Nvidia also shares in a portion of the Neocloud’s revenue earned above the backstop level.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis reports that NVIDIA has started providing neoclouds with take-or-pay minimum-revenue guarantees on GPU capacity in exchange for a share of revenue above the backstop level.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: Here, Nvidia is diving even deeper, as it has started backstopping datacenter leases.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis reports that NVIDIA has also started backstopping data-center leases.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: Nvidia’s backstop program is typically six years in length, and during these six years, Nvidia stands ready to purchase compute at pre-agreed price levels that vary over the time period.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis says NVIDIA’s backstop agreements typically run for six years and require it to stand ready to buy compute at pre-agreed prices that vary over the term.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: The below table is an illustrative example to explain the basic terms of the program – we present a backstop pricing curve that we believe to be on the lower end of the backstop range – in this case at an average of $2.36 over the six-year period, but we expect that most Neoclouds will negotiate higher backstops.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis models an illustrative low-end NVIDIA backstop averaging $2.36 per GPU-hour over six years and expects most neoclouds to negotiate higher backstop prices.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: In the case where Nvidia earns 40% revenue share, we see that in year 1, the Neocloud will charge its customers $6.75/hr on average. Of this, the Neocloud earns the full amount up to Nvidia’s year 1 backstop of $3.68/hr, but for the difference between $6.75/hr charged to customers and the $3.68/hr backstop amounting to $3.07/hr, Nvidia will earn $1.23/hr and the Neocloud will earn $1.84/hr. In total, the Neocloud will realize $5.52/hr for the first year, which of course is lower than the $6.75/hr that they would have earned without the backstop. Over the six years of this scenario, the Nvidia take rate works out to be about 18% on average, but without the backstop, there would be no cluster!
evidence.one_line: In SemiAnalysis’s illustrative model, with a 40% share of revenue above the backstop, NVIDIA receives $1.23 per GPU-hour in year one and takes about 18% of the neocloud’s revenue over six years; the neocloud realizes $5.52 per hour in year one.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: We see that the short-term 1y rental book scenario clearly offers the best IRR among the backstopped scenarios at 25.4%, and these IRRs could realize even higher if the rental market turns out to be strong enough such that 1y and shorter rental rates decay by less than we modeled in the curve below. As expected, the IRRs are higher without a backstop – reaching as high as 40.7% when renting for 1y tenors with no backstop. But if Neoclouds activate the backstop and rent to Nvidia at those prices, they can expect to earn zero or negative IRRs.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis models a 25.4% IRR for a neocloud’s one-year-rental book with an NVIDIA backstop, up to 40.7% without a backstop, and zero or negative IRRs if the backstop is activated at the modeled prices.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: Readers may notice the huge gap between CoreWeave 5y unsecured bonds at ~10% and the 5.9% that CoreWeave paid for the fixed-rate tranche of their DDTL 4.0 $8.5B delayed-draw term loan, which was backstopped by Meta. This 5.9% yield works out to about 90 basis points wider than Meta’s 5y bond yield of ~5.0%. This can be interpreted as the market pricing CoreWeave’s execution risk with respect to that particular project at 90bps.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis calculates that CoreWeave’s 5.9% yield on the fixed-rate tranche of its $8.5 billion Meta-backstopped delayed-draw loan was about 90 basis points above Meta’s roughly 5.0% five-year bond yield, versus roughly 10% on CoreWeave’s unsecured bonds.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: In our modelling, we show that increasing funding from an all-in cost of 5.62% to an all-in cost of 10% drops PBT margins from 14.8% down to only 5.4%.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis models that raising a neocloud’s all-in funding cost from 5.62% to 10% reduces its pretax-profit margin from 14.8% to 5.4%.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: When it comes to the Nvidia backstop, banks look at the DSCR ratios assuming revenue earned under the scenario where the backstop is activated. They are looking for a DSCR of at least 1.3x, particularly for the first few years of GPU financing agreement and size their loans to ensure that this bar is met. This typically corresponds to a 70-80% loan to value (LTV) ratio.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis says lenders size NVIDIA-backstopped GPU loans to achieve at least 1.3x debt-service coverage in the backstop-activated scenario, typically corresponding to 70–80% loan-to-value.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: We think that initial lending will be at a wider spread than the current 5y backstopped hyperscale deals which come in at around SOFR + 225bps (roughly equivalent to a Z-spread of 195bps, or about 5.9% total yield) but at a tighter spread than CoreWeave’s 5-year unsecured corporate bond which has a yield of ~10% (roughly equivalent to Z-spread of 600bps).
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis expects initial lending to neoclouds to price wider than five-year hyperscaler-backstopped deals at about 5.9% yield, but tighter than CoreWeave’s five-year unsecured bonds at about 10%.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis
